features.definition: The most the policy pays for surgery costs, per person per year.
features.why: Surgery is the biggest bill private insurance exists to pay — this cap (or its absence) is the ceiling on that protection.

features.definition: The cap on hospital treatment that isn't surgery (e.g. medical admissions).
What you can choose to pay yourself per claim/year in exchange for lower premiums.
features.why: What you pay before the insurer does — and per-year vs per-claim changes the maths of a bad year.

features.definition: What cancer treatment is covered and up to how much.
Cover for effective drugs NZ's public system doesn't fund — one of the biggest real differences between NZ policies.
features.why: Modern medicines Pharmac doesn't fund can cost six figures a year — this line decides who pays for them.

features.definition: Cover for surveillance/check-ups after cancer treatment.
Cover for private specialist visits — capped amount, and whether GP referral is required.
MRI, CT, and other tests — what's covered, any caps, any time-link to surgery.
Whether tests/consultations must relate to treatment within a set window to be claimable.
How each insurer treats conditions you had before joining — excluded, covered after a period, or reviewable.
features.why: What you already have is priced or excluded when you join — the biggest reason timing matters in insurance.

features.definition: How long after joining before specific benefits can be claimed.
Whether and when conditions present from birth are covered.
features.why: Conditions present from birth are excluded by most policies; the exceptions differ insurer to insurer.

features.definition: Optional module for everyday costs: GP visits, prescriptions, dental, optical.
features.why: Everyday costs — GP, prescriptions, dental — are optional extras with very different shapes and caps.

features.definition: Any cover for pregnancy-related care.
features.why: Pregnancy-related cover ranges from a modest allowance to a full exclusion.

features.definition: Any cover for psychiatric/psychological care.
features.why: Cover for psychiatrists, psychologists and counselling ranges from a base-plan benefit to a total exclusion.

features.definition: Remote GP/specialist consultations covered or provided.
Caps and lists for implants and devices used in surgery.
Whether you must use the insurer's affiliated providers for full cover.
Whether treatment must be approved before you book it.
How claims are made and typical settlement approach.
Extra benefits that accrue the longer you hold the policy.
features.why: Benefits that unlock with tenure — and reset to zero if you switch insurers.

features.definition: How premiums change with age/claims (community-rated vs age-rated).
Whether improvements to the policy automatically apply to existing members.
The main things this policy will never pay for.
Any age at which cover ends or changes.

glossary.excess: The amount you pay yourself when you claim, before the insurer pays the rest. A higher excess means cheaper premiums.
glossary.Pharmac: New Zealand's government drug-funding agency — it decides which medicines the public system pays for.
glossary.non-Pharmac: A medicine approved as safe for use in NZ (by Medsafe) but not publicly funded — you pay for it, unless your insurance covers it.
glossary.Medsafe: The NZ regulator that approves medicines as safe and legal to prescribe. Approval doesn't mean public funding — that's Pharmac.
glossary.pre-existing condition: Any health condition, sign or symptom you had before taking out the policy. Usually excluded or priced in when you join.
glossary.underwriting: The insurer's assessment of your health when you apply — it decides your exclusions, loadings and price.
glossary.stand-down period: A waiting period after joining before a specific benefit can be claimed.
glossary.congenital condition: A condition present from birth (or diagnosed soon after), whether inherited or not. Most policies exclude these.
glossary.prostheses: Surgically implanted devices — hip joints, heart valves, lenses. Policies often cap what they'll pay per item.
glossary.reasonable charges: The insurer's benchmark for what a treatment should cost. Charges above it may leave you paying the gap.
glossary.policy wording: The legal document that decides what's actually covered. Marketing pages summarise; the wording rules.
glossary.specialist: A vocationally registered medical specialist (e.g. surgeon, oncologist). Most benefits require specialist involvement or referral.
glossary.loyalty benefit: Extra cover that unlocks after years of continuous membership — and resets if you switch insurers.
glossary.policy year: The 12 months your benefit limits apply to, resetting at renewal. Also called a claims year.
glossary.prior approval: Asking the insurer to confirm cover before treatment. Skipping it can mean paying first and arguing later.
